title: Citadel Buys Situational Awareness Stock Portfolio After AI Fund's Collapse
excerpt: Ken Griffin's hedge fund acquires the leveraged portion of Leopold Aschenbrenner's AI-focused portfolio after the former OpenAI researcher's fund was battered by July's tech selloff, triggering relief buying across Wall Street.
body:
• Situational Awareness sold the bulk of its public stock portfolio to Citadel after heavy losses in the AI stock rout, with Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citigroup facilitating the deal.
  • The fund, which posted a 439% return in the first half of 2026 and had assets as high as $45 billion, used up to 4x leverage on its AI bets — amplifying losses when the market turned.
  • Situational retains roughly $10 billion in holdings, including its private stake in Anthropic, while Citadel acquired only the broker-financed portion of the portfolio.
  • News of the forced sale triggered immediate relief buying in AI stocks, with traders betting the removal of a major seller signals the bottom may be near.

Situational Awareness, the AI-focused hedge fund founded by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, has sold the bulk of its public equities portfolio to Ken Griffin's Citadel after suffering deep losses during July's brutal tech selloff, according to reports from Reuters and the Wall Street Journal citing people familiar with the matter.

The deal marks a sudden and dramatic reversal for one of the fastest-growing hedge funds in recent memory — a fund that had turned Aschenbrenner, still in his mid-20s, into something of a Wall Street celebrity.

From 2,000% Returns to Forced Liquidation

Situational Awareness launched in September 2024 and quickly became one of the most watched funds on Wall Street. Using heavy leverage to place concentrated bets on AI and semiconductor stocks, the fund posted staggering returns — more than 2,000% since inception and 439% in the first half of 2026 alone, according to the Financial Times.

At its peak in early July, the fund's assets under management climbed as high as $45 billion, CNBC reported. Its portfolio included sizable positions in Broadcom, Intel, CoreWeave, SK Hynix, SanDisk, Bloom Energy, Nebius Group, Nvidia, Oracle, and AMD, according to regulatory filings.

But the same leverage that supercharged returns — at times as high as four times the fund's underlying capital — became a liability when AI stocks began cratering. As holdings plunged, the fund faced pressure to either raise fresh capital or offload its positions to meet margin demands from lenders.

"Speculation had been out there in the market all week that Situational Awareness was potentially under pressure, obviously a lot of names in their portfolio had been sold aggressively."

— Michael O'Rourke, Chief Market Strategist, Jones Trading

How the Deal Was Structured

Citadel, which manages roughly $71 billion in assets, acquired the portion of Situational's public stock portfolio that had been financed with borrowed money from prime brokers, Reuters reported. Situational retains approximately $10 billion in holdings, including stocks funded by client capital and private investments such as its stake in AI giant Anthropic.

Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citigroup helped facilitate the block trade between the two firms. Millennium Management had also bid on the portfolio but did not end up participating, according to Bloomberg.

Aschenbrenner had attracted prominent backers during the fund's rapid ascent, including secretive trading firm Jane Street, Stripe co-founders Patrick and John Collison, and Meta Platforms executives Daniel Gross and Nat Friedman.

A Broader AI Reckoning

The forced sale didn't happen in a vacuum. Global hedge funds are facing their biggest monthly drawdown on record as AI stocks have been hammered across the board. Asia-focused long-short funds are down 18.6% on average through July 28, according to a Goldman Sachs prime brokerage note. A widely followed Goldman Sachs long-short basket of high-beta momentum names dropped nearly 40% for the month.

Morgan Stanley's prime brokerage unit noted that stock-picking hedge funds have been rushing to unwind AI positions, covering shorts and selling longs in roughly equal measure — a classic sign of forced deleveraging rather than a fundamental reassessment.

Relief Rally — or False Bottom?

Within hours of CNBC breaking the news that Situational had dumped its leveraged positions via a block trade, a wave of relief buying swept through the fund's former holdings. With the overhang of a major forced seller removed, traders piled back into beaten-down AI names.

"When you know that a potential seller is out of the market — that's when all the buy-the-dippers come rushing back in."

— Michael O'Rourke, Chief Market Strategist, Jones Trading

Whether this marks a genuine turning point for the AI trade remains an open question. Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, urged caution.

"Almost every massive inflection point comes with one of these stories, but very few of these stories leads to a massive inflection point," Hackett told MarketWatch.

What Comes Next

For Situational Awareness, the immediate crisis has passed but the damage is considerable. The fund still holds its Anthropic position and other private investments, but its public equities operation — the engine of those headline-grabbing returns — has been effectively wound down.

For the broader market, the episode is a textbook case of how leverage amplifies both gains and losses. The AI trade that minted fortunes over the past two years has now claimed one of its highest-profile casualties. Whether Citadel's willingness to buy at distressed prices proves prescient — or premature — will be one of the key stories to watch in the second half of 2026.
